texts.title: EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow".
texts.text: High-quality training data play a key role in image segmentation tasks. Usually, pixel-level annotations are expensive, laborious and time-consuming for the large size of segmentation datasets. Interactive segmentation has been widely adopted to reduce the annotation cost, in which a user provides a few clicks to indicate foreground and background regions and the model predicts the object mask iteratively. However, existing interactive frameworks still suffer from two limitations: the interactive information is not fully exploited during propagation through the network, and many methods rely on heavy post-processing or iterative optimization schemes to refine boundaries, which makes them impractical for real annotation scenarios. In this paper, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel interactive architecture that makes full use of interactive information of user clicks with edge-guided flow. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance without any post-processing or iterative optimization scheme. Specifically, an edge mask is predicted by an edge-guided branch and fed back as guidance to a coarse-to-fine network, so that click cues and boundary cues are jointly propagated and progressively refined. Comprehensive experiments on benchmarks, including GrabCut, Berkeley, SBD and DAVIS, demonstrate the superiority of our method over prior work in terms of the number of clicks required to reach a target IoU. In addition, with the proposed method, we develop an efficient interactive segmentation tool for practical data annotation tasks. The source code and the annotation tool are available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

texts.title: Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning".
texts.text: Few-shot segmentation aims to segment objects of previously unseen classes in a query image given only a handful of annotated support examples. Most existing approaches compress the support annotations into one or a few class prototypes and match them against query features, but this compression discards spatial detail and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to the large appearance gap that frequently separates support and query instances of the same class. Moreover, because the encoder is trained on abundant base classes, its embedding space tends to be organized around base-class semantics and transfers poorly to novel categories. We propose a framework that couples global and local contrastive learning to build an embedding space that is both class-discriminative and spatially precise. The global branch contrasts episode-level class representations, pulling support and query features of the same category together while pushing apart representations of different categories across the training set, which reduces intra-class bias and yields prototypes that generalize beyond the base classes. The local branch performs dense, pixel-level contrast within each episode, separating foreground from background embeddings and sharpening object boundaries that prototype matching alone tends to blur. The two objectives are optimized jointly with the standard segmentation loss and require no additional annotation or inference-time cost. Experiments on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i show consistent gains over strong prototype-based baselines in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, and ablations confirm that the global and local terms contribute complementary improvements, with the largest benefit on classes exhibiting wide appearance variation.

texts.title: Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: The success of deep learning methods in medical image segmentation tasks usually comes at the cost of extensive labeling of the target dataset, which is expensive and time-consuming to acquire because it demands scarce expert knowledge and pixel-level annotation of volumetric scans. Contrastive learning offers a way to exploit abundant unlabeled data, but conventional formulations treat every other image as a negative sample, which is problematic in medical imaging: scans from different patients share highly consistent anatomy, so semantically identical regions are repeatedly pushed apart, and the resulting representations transfer poorly to dense prediction. In this work we propose a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework that couples supervision from a small labeled set with a label-aware contrastive objective defined at the pixel and region level. The limited annotations, together with confident pseudo-labels produced by a mean-teacher model, are used to identify positive pairs across images that belong to the same anatomical class, while a class-aware sampling strategy prevents dominant background regions from overwhelming the loss. Contrastive representation learning and segmentation training are optimized jointly rather than sequentially, so the embedding space is shaped by the downstream objective throughout training. We evaluate our method on cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and prostate MRI segmentation benchmarks. With only 5-10% of the labels, the proposed method consistently outperforms supervised baselines and recent semi-supervised and self-supervised approaches, recovering a large fraction of fully supervised performance and yielding the largest gains for small and low-contrast structures. Ablations confirm that both label-aware positive mining and joint optimization are necessary for these improvements.

texts.title: A Spatial Guided Self-supervised Clustering Network for Medical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "A Spatial Guided Self-supervised Clustering Network for Medical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: The use of hand-crafted features and supervised deep learning for medical image segmentation is constrained by the limited availability of large, carefully annotated datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to produce and often require domain expertise. Self-supervised learning offers a way to learn feature representations directly from unlabelled data, but existing self-supervised clustering methods were designed for natural images and mainly optimise pixel-level feature similarity; they neglect the spatial relationships between pixels and therefore tend to produce fragmented, noisy regions when applied to medical images, where tissue boundaries are indistinct and intensity distributions overlap. We propose a Spatial Guided Self-supervised Clustering Network (SGSCN) for medical image segmentation, which iteratively learns feature representations and cluster assignments for every pixel in an end-to-end fashion from a single image. Our method introduces a spatial consistency loss that encourages spatially adjacent pixels with similar appearance to share the same cluster, thereby preserving compact and coherent anatomical structures, together with a context-based consistency loss that constrains the learned representations to remain stable under transformations of the same image, yielding more discriminative and robust features. We evaluated our method on two public medical image datasets, a skin lesion dataset and a chest X-ray dataset, where it consistently outperformed conventional unsupervised methods and state-of-the-art self-supervised segmentation approaches.

texts.title: Iterative, Deep, and Unsupervised Synthetic Aperture Sonar Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Iterative, Deep, and Unsupervised Synthetic Aperture Sonar Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) produces high-resolution imagery of the seafloor over wide swaths, and partitioning that imagery into regions of coherent seafloor texture is a prerequisite for downstream tasks such as target detection, change detection, and habitat mapping. Supervised segmentation is difficult to apply in this domain: seafloor classes are not sharply delineated, human labeling of SAS imagery is slow and inconsistent, and the resulting label sets rarely transfer across sonars, frequencies, or survey geometries. We present an iterative, deep, and unsupervised framework for SAS image segmentation that requires no human-annotated masks. The method alternates between two steps: a deep network is trained to predict cluster assignments from image patches, and the assignments are then re-estimated by clustering the network's learned feature representations. Repeating this alternation lets the representation and the partition refine one another, progressively sharpening class structure that a single pass of feature extraction followed by clustering does not recover. A superpixel-based refinement stage aligns the resulting pixel-level labeling with image boundaries and suppresses spurious speckle-induced fragmentation. We evaluate the approach on a large real-world SAS dataset collected over varied seafloor types, and additionally on natural imagery to show that the framework is not specific to sonar. Against unsupervised and self-supervised baselines, the proposed method yields partitions that agree more closely with expert-designated seafloor regions, and an ablation study isolates the contributions of the iterative scheme and the superpixel refinement.

texts.title: Double Similarity Distillation for Semantic Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Double Similarity Distillation for Semantic Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Recently, most semantic segmentation methods have achieved impressive performance by relying on deep networks with heavy computation and large memory footprints, which restricts their deployment on resource-constrained platforms. Knowledge distillation offers a promising way to obtain compact yet accurate segmentation models, but existing approaches mainly transfer knowledge distilled from a single level or from isolated pixel pairs, and therefore fail to exploit the rich structural relations that characterize dense prediction. In this paper, we propose a double similarity distillation (DSD) framework to improve the classification accuracy of all existing compact segmentation networks from two complementary perspectives. Specifically, we first design a pixel-wise similarity distillation (PSD) module, which utilizes residual attention maps to capture more detailed spatial dependencies across multiple layers, so that the student network inherits the fine-grained spatial structure encoded by the teacher. Considering the global category correlation in semantic segmentation, we then propose a category-wise similarity distillation (CSD) module, which builds the correlation matrix over category representations and transfers the resulting relational knowledge, thereby strengthening the consistency of the student's category-level responses. Extensive experiments on four challenging benchmarks, including Cityscapes, CamVid, ADE20K, and Pascal VOC 2012, demonstrate that the proposed DSD framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods for semantic segmentation without increasing inference cost.

texts.title: Attention-Based 3D Seismic Fault Segmentation Training by a Few 2D Slice Labels
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Attention-Based 3D Seismic Fault Segmentation Training by a Few 2D Slice Labels".
texts.text: Delineating faults from seismic volumes is a labor-intensive step of subsurface interpretation, and although deep learning has made 3D fault segmentation far more efficient, its practical use remains limited by the cost of producing dense, volumetric ground truth. Fully annotating a 3D seismic cube is prohibitively time-consuming, while synthetic training data, though cheap to generate, encodes simplified structural and noise statistics that do not transfer reliably to field surveys. In this paper we show that a 3D fault segmentation network can be trained effectively from only a handful of sparsely annotated 2D slices drawn from the target volume. We propose an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture in which residual attention modules and channel-spatial attention gates suppress responses from stratigraphic reflectors and acquisition noise while amplifying thin, laterally discontinuous fault signatures, addressing the severe foreground-background imbalance that characterizes fault labels. To exploit incomplete supervision, we introduce a masked loss formulation that back-propagates only through labeled slices, combined with a binary cross-entropy and Dice objective, so that unlabeled voxels contribute no spurious negative gradients. Training is performed directly on the survey of interest, allowing the network to adapt to its particular wavelet, resolution, and noise characteristics. Experiments on public field datasets, including the Netherlands F3 and Kerry-3D surveys, show that networks trained with fewer than ten labeled slices produce fault probability volumes that are more continuous, less noisy, and better aligned with interpreter picks than coherence-based attributes and synthetically trained baselines, while requiring a small fraction of the annotation effort.

texts.title: Comprehensive Multi-Modal Interactions for Referring Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Comprehensive Multi-Modal Interactions for Referring Image Segmentation".
texts.text: We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a segmentation map corresponding to the natural language description. Addressing RIS efficiently requires considering the interactions happening across visual and linguistic modalities and the interactions within each modality. Existing methods are limited because they either compute different forms of interactions sequentially (leading to error propagation) or ignore intra-modal interactions. We address this limitation by performing all three interactions simultaneously through a Synchronous Multi-Modal Fusion Module (SFM). Moreover, to produce refined segmentation masks, we propose a novel Hierarchical Cross-Modal Aggregation Module (HCAM), where linguistic features facilitate the exchange of contextual information across the visual hierarchy. We present thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.

texts.title: FUTURE-AI: Guiding Principles and Consensus Recommendations for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Future Medical Imaging
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "FUTURE-AI: Guiding Principles and Consensus Recommendations for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Future Medical Imaging".
texts.text: The recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) combined with the extensive amount of data generated by today's clinical systems, has led to the development of imaging AI solutions across the whole value chain of medical imaging, including image reconstruction, medical image segmentation, image-based diagnosis and treatment planning. Notwithstanding the successes and future potential of AI in medical imaging, many stakeholders are concerned of the potential risks and ethical implications of imaging AI solutions, which are perceived as complex, opaque, and difficult to comprehend, utilise, and trust in critical clinical applications. Despite these concerns and risks, there are currently no concrete guidelines and best practices for guiding future AI developments in medical imaging towards increased trust, safety and adoption. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a careful selection of guiding principles drawn from the accumulated experiences, consensus, and best practices from five large European projects on AI in Health Imaging. These guiding principles are named FUTURE-AI and its building blocks consist of (i) Fairness, (ii) Universality, (iii) Traceability, (iv) Usability, (v) Robustness and (vi) Explainability. In a step-by-step approach, these guidelines are further translated into a framework of concrete recommendations for specifying, developing, evaluating and deploying technically, clinically and ethically trustworthy AI solutions into clinical practice.

texts.title: Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation".
texts.text: Image segmentation is often ambiguous at the level of individual image patches and requires contextual information to reach consistent label agreement. In this paper we introduce an approach for semantic segmentation based purely on transformers. Building on recent work on vision transformers (ViT), we treat semantic segmentation as a sequence-to-sequence problem and use a transformer encoder to produce contextualized patch embeddings, capturing global image context at every layer of the model. In contrast to convolutional architectures, whose receptive field grows only gradually with depth and which rely on additional modules to aggregate context, our encoder models long-range interactions from the first layer onward. We then decode these embeddings to per-pixel class scores with either a simple pointwise linear decoder or a mask transformer decoder, in which learnable class embeddings are jointly processed with patch embeddings and produce segmentation masks through a scalar product. Our method, Segmenter, is simple and flexible: it can be initialized from models pretrained for image classification and instantiated at different model and patch sizes to trade off accuracy against runtime. We study these trade-offs and show that our approach outperforms the state of the art on ADE20K and Pascal Context while performing competitively on Cityscapes.

texts.title: Mining Contextual Information Beyond Image for Semantic Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Mining Contextual Information Beyond Image for Semantic Segmentation".
texts.text: This paper studies the context aggregation problem in semantic image segmentation. The existing researches focus on improving the pixel representations by aggregating the contextual information within individual images. Though impressive, these methods neglect the significance of the representations of the pixels of the corresponding class beyond the input image. To address this, this paper proposes to mine the contextual information beyond individual images to further augment the pixel representations. We first set up a feature memory module, which is updated dynamically during training, to store the dataset-level representations of various categories. Then, we learn class probability distribution of each pixel representation under the supervision of the ground-truth segmentation. At last, the representation of each pixel is augmented by aggregating the dataset-level representations based on the corresponding class probability distribution. Furthermore, by utilizing the stored dataset-level representations, we also propose a representation consistent learning strategy to make the classification head better address intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. The proposed method could be effortlessly incorporated into existing segmentation frameworks (e.g., FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet and DeepLabV3) and brings consistent performance improvements. Mining contextual information beyond image allows us to report state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks: ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff.

texts.title: Combo Loss: Handling Input and Output Imbalance in Multi-Organ Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Combo Loss: Handling Input and Output Imbalance in Multi-Organ Segmentation".
texts.text: Simultaneous segmentation of multiple organs from different medical imaging modalities is a crucial task as it can be exploited for computerized diagnosis, treatment planning, and quantitative follow-up. However, learning-based approaches to this problem are hampered by two distinct forms of imbalance. The first, input imbalance, arises because the organs of interest occupy only a small fraction of the image volume and differ greatly in size among themselves, so that gradient contributions from large structures and from background voxels dominate training. The second, output imbalance, refers to the unequal cost of the two error types at inference: depending on the clinical application, an over-segmented boundary and an under-segmented one carry very different penalties, yet standard objectives treat false positives and false negatives symmetrically. We propose Combo loss, a curriculum-free objective that linearly combines a Dice-based term, which supervises the model at the level of region overlap, with a modified cross-entropy term whose per-class weighting explicitly trades off false positives against false negatives. The formulation exposes two interpretable coefficients that let the practitioner tune the relative influence of the overlap and distribution terms and steer the operating point of the resulting segmentation without changing the network architecture. We evaluate Combo loss against Dice, weighted and focal cross-entropy, Tversky, and exponential logarithmic losses on multi-organ and lesion segmentation tasks in CT and MRI, using several fully convolutional backbones. Combo loss yields consistently higher Dice scores, improved robustness for small structures, and more stable convergence, while requiring no additional computation at test time.

texts.title: Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets".
texts.text: While improving predictive accuracy has been the focus of much of machine learning in recent years, accuracy alone does not suffice for reliable decision-making. Deploying learning systems in consequential settings also requires calibrating and communicating the uncertainty of predictions. To convey instance-wise uncertainty for prediction tasks, we show how to generate set-valued predictions from a black-box predictor that control the expected loss on future test points at a user-specified level. Our approach provides explicit finite-sample guarantees for any dataset by using a holdout set to calibrate the size of the prediction sets. This framework enables simple, distribution-free, rigorous error control for many tasks, and we demonstrate it in five large-scale machine learning problems: (1) classification problems where some mistakes are more costly than others; (2) multi-label classification, where each observation has multiple associated labels; (3) classification problems where the labels have a hierarchical structure; (4) image segmentation, where we wish to predict a set of pixels containing an object of interest; and (5) protein structure prediction. Lastly, we discuss extensions to uncertainty quantification for ranking, metric learning, and distributionally robust learning.

texts.title: Segmentation in Style: Unsupervised Semantic Image Segmentation with Stylegan and CLIP
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Segmentation in Style: Unsupervised Semantic Image Segmentation with Stylegan and CLIP".
texts.text: We present a method for segmenting images into semantically meaningful regions without any human annotation. Our approach exploits the observation that a pretrained StyleGAN generator encodes rich, spatially localized semantics in its intermediate feature maps: activations that belong to the same object part tend to cluster together, both within an image and consistently across the generated distribution. We first sample a large collection of images from the generator, collect their multi-resolution intermediate activations, and cluster these features to obtain a set of candidate semantic classes together with per-pixel pseudo-labels. The resulting labeled samples are then used to train a lightweight segmentation head, which can be applied either to generated images or, through an encoder that inverts real images into the latent space, to arbitrary photographs at inference time. Because the discovered regions are defined by the generator rather than by a taxonomy, their granularity and grouping need not match the classes a user has in mind. To address this, we make the discovery process controllable through natural language: using CLIP, we score each discovered cluster against a textual description of the region of interest and merge or select clusters accordingly, so that the final segmentation reflects a user-specified concept without requiring a single labeled mask. Experiments on face, animal, and vehicle datasets show that the unsupervised clusters correspond closely to human-defined parts, that the learned segmentation head transfers to real images, and that text guidance reliably steers the output toward the requested concept. Our method achieves competitive performance against prior unsupervised and few-shot segmentation approaches while requiring no pixel-level supervision, and it offers a practical way to obtain segmentation models for domains where annotation is expensive or the class definition is itself uncertain.

texts.title: Towards Robust General Medical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Towards Robust General Medical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: The reliability of Deep Learning systems depends on their accuracy but also on their robustness against adversarial perturbations to the input data. Several attacks and defenses have been proposed to improve the performance of Deep Neural Networks under the presence of adversarial noise in the natural image domain. However, robustness in computer-aided diagnosis for volumetric data has only been explored for specific tasks and with limited attacks. We propose a new framework to assess the robustness of general medical image segmentation systems. Our contributions are two-fold: (i) we introduce a new benchmark to evaluate robustness in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) by extending the recent AutoAttack natural image classification framework to the domain of volumetric data segmentation, and (ii) we present a novel lattice architecture for RObust Generic medical image segmentation (ROG). Our results show that ROG is capable of generalizing across different tasks of the MSD and largely surpasses the state-of-the-art under sophisticated adversarial attacks.

texts.title: Efficient and Generic Interactive Segmentation Framework to Correct Mispredictions during Clinical Evaluation of Medical Images
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Efficient and Generic Interactive Segmentation Framework to Correct Mispredictions during Clinical Evaluation of Medical Images".
texts.text: Deep learning models for medical image segmentation now reach expert-level accuracy on many benchmarks, yet they still fail in ways that matter clinically: boundaries leak into adjacent structures, small or low-contrast lesions are missed, and performance degrades on scanners, protocols, and pathologies not represented in training data. Because a clinician cannot accept a segmentation that is locally wrong, correcting such mispredictions at the point of evaluation is a prerequisite for deployment. Existing interactive segmentation methods address this only partially: they typically train a dedicated interactive network from scratch, couple the correction mechanism tightly to one backbone, or rely on per-case test-time optimization, all of which are costly and must be redone whenever the underlying model changes. We propose an interactive segmentation framework that is both efficient and generic. It attaches to any already-trained segmentation network without altering or retraining its weights, encodes sparse user input (clicks or scribbles) into a spatial guidance representation, and refines the prediction through a lightweight module that operates on the frozen network's features, so each correction requires a single fast forward pass rather than an optimization loop. Training uses simulated interactions derived from the base model's own error modes, which concentrates capacity on the mistakes that actually occur. We evaluate the framework across several public CT and MRI datasets and multiple backbone architectures, showing that it reaches a target segmentation quality with fewer user interactions and substantially lower computational and memory cost than representative interactive baselines, while leaving the base model's automatic performance intact. The framework therefore offers a practical route to clinician-in-the-loop correction in existing segmentation pipelines.

texts.title: Semi-supervised Left Atrium Segmentation with Mutual Consistency Training
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semi-supervised Left Atrium Segmentation with Mutual Consistency Training".
texts.text: Semi-supervised learning has attracted growing attention in medical image segmentation, since dense annotations of three-dimensional scans are costly and require expert knowledge. A central difficulty is that the regions a model finds hardest to delineate, such as thin, ambiguous or low-contrast boundaries, are exactly the regions where unreliable predictions on unlabeled data can reinforce their own errors. We argue that such challenging regions can be located by the disagreement between different views of the same model, and that this disagreement provides a useful training signal. We therefore propose a mutual consistency network (MC-Net) for semi-supervised left atrium segmentation from 3D magnetic resonance images. MC-Net consists of a shared encoder and two slightly different decoders; the statistical discrepancy between the two decoder outputs is used as an estimate of model uncertainty, highlighting unlabeled voxels where segmentation is hard. We then design a cycled pseudo-label scheme in which the soft prediction of each decoder is converted into a pseudo label that supervises the other decoder, encouraging the two branches to agree on low-confidence regions and thereby learning generalizable features from unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on the Left Atrium database show that MC-Net outperforms recent semi-supervised methods, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with limited labeled scans. Code is publicly available.

texts.title: CHASE: Robust Visual Tracking via Cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "CHASE: Robust Visual Tracking via Cell-Level Differentiable Neural Architecture Search".
texts.text: A strong feature representation is the cornerstone of modern visual tracking, yet the backbone and neck architectures of state-of-the-art Siamese trackers are still borrowed from image classification networks and hand-tuned for the tracking task. Such manual adaptation is expensive, relies heavily on expert intuition, and yields designs that are rarely optimal for the target–search matching problem, particularly under occlusion, deformation, scale variation, and background clutter. We propose CHASE, a cell-level differentiable architecture search framework that automates the design of the adaptation module in Siamese trackers rather than the backbone itself. CHASE relaxes the discrete space of operations and their connections into a continuous one and learns, by gradient descent, a compact cell that refines and aligns the features of a fixed pre-trained backbone for correlation-based matching. Because the search is confined to a single cell and the backbone remains frozen, the method is memory- and time-efficient, and the resulting cell is architecture-agnostic: it can be plugged into different tracking pipelines without redesigning the rest of the network. Extensive experiments on OTB2015, VOT2019, UAV123, LaSOT, TrackingNet, and GOT-10k show that CHASE consistently improves the robustness and accuracy of its baseline trackers and performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods while running in real time.

texts.title: Large-scale image segmentation based on distributed clustering algorithms
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Large-scale image segmentation based on distributed clustering algorithms".
texts.text: Image segmentation is a fundamental step in scene interpretation, but classical clustering-based formulations scale poorly: as image size grows from megapixels to gigapixels, the pixel- or object-level feature sets exceed the memory of a single machine, and the iterative distance computations that dominate clustering become prohibitively slow. This paper presents a distributed framework for segmenting very large images by reformulating clustering-based segmentation as a data-parallel computation. The image is decomposed into overlapping tiles that are distributed across a compute cluster, local features (spectral, textural, and spatial) are extracted in parallel, and cluster assignment and centroid update steps are expressed as map and reduce operations so that only compact sufficient statistics, rather than raw pixel data, are exchanged between nodes. To avoid the boundary artifacts introduced by naive tiling, we add a global centroid synchronization step and a border-region reconciliation procedure that merges segments spanning adjacent tiles under a region-adjacency criterion. We further reduce communication cost through scalable seeding and mini-batch updates. Experiments on high-resolution remote sensing and biomedical imagery show that the distributed implementation produces segmentations essentially equivalent to the centralized baseline, as measured by boundary recall and region consistency, while achieving near-linear speedup with the number of nodes and enabling the segmentation of images that cannot be processed on a single workstation.

texts.title: Transformer Meets Convolution: A Bilateral Awareness Net-work for Semantic Segmentation of Very Fine Resolution Ur-ban Scene Images
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Transformer Meets Convolution: A Bilateral Awareness Net-work for Semantic Segmentation of Very Fine Resolution Ur-ban Scene Images".
texts.text: Semantic segmentation of very fine resolution (VFR) urban scene imagery is a fundamental task for applications such as land-cover mapping, urban planning, and change detection. However, VFR images pose two coupled difficulties: the enlarged intra-class variance and reduced inter-class variance of ground objects demand long-range contextual reasoning, while the abundance of fine structural detail—building edges, narrow roads, small vehicles—demands the preservation of precise spatial information. Conventional convolutional neural networks, constrained by the local receptive field of the convolution operator, capture global dependencies only indirectly through deep stacking and aggressive downsampling, which in turn erodes the spatial detail that VFR imagery uniquely provides. In this paper, we propose a Bilateral Awareness Network (BANet) that couples the complementary strengths of the Transformer and the convolution. BANet comprises two parallel paths: a dependency path built upon a lightweight, efficient Transformer backbone that models long-range contextual dependencies and global semantic relationships, and a texture path composed of shallow convolutional layers that retains high-resolution, fine-grained spatial and boundary detail. Because the two paths encode information of markedly different granularity and semantic level, a feature aggregation module (FAM) is designed to bridge them, employing a combination of channel attention and spatial attention to adaptively reweight and fuse the dependency and texture representations rather than merging them by naive summation or concatenation. Extensive experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets—the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam 2D semantic labelling datasets and the UAVid dataset. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that BANet achieves competitive or superior accuracy in comparison with state-of-the-art lightweight segmentation networks while maintaining an efficient speed–accuracy trade-off, confirming the effectiveness of jointly exploiting global dependency modelling and local texture preservation for VFR urban scene segmentation.

texts.title: Trilateral Attention Network for Real-time Medical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Trilateral Attention Network for Real-time Medical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Accurate delineation of anatomical structures and lesions is a prerequisite for computer-assisted diagnosis and intraoperative guidance, yet the most accurate segmentation networks remain too heavy for the latency budgets of clinical workstations and point-of-care devices. Encoder-decoder architectures recover spatial detail through dense skip connections, while transformer-based models capture long-range context at quadratic cost; both trade throughput for accuracy, and both tend to blur the thin, low-contrast boundaries that dominate clinical error. We propose the Trilateral Attention Network (TANet), a real-time segmentation architecture that factorizes representation learning into three lightweight, mutually attentive pathways: a high-resolution detail path that preserves fine structure at shallow depth, a semantic path that aggregates global context through strided depthwise convolutions and linear-complexity self-attention, and a boundary path supervised by distance-transform targets that explicitly models organ and lesion contours. A trilateral fusion module exchanges information across the three pathways using cross-path channel and spatial gating, allowing boundary evidence to sharpen semantic predictions without reintroducing dense high-resolution computation. We evaluate TANet on four public benchmarks spanning endoscopic polyp imaging, cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and dermoscopy. TANet attains competitive or superior Dice scores relative to recent heavyweight baselines while running at 97 FPS on a single consumer GPU with 4.1M parameters, and it yields consistent improvements in Hausdorff distance, indicating better boundary fidelity. Ablations isolate the contribution of each pathway and of cross-path gating, and cross-center experiments show that the boundary path improves robustness under acquisition shift. Code and trained models will be released.

texts.title: ComBiNet: Compact Convolutional Bayesian Neural Network for Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "ComBiNet: Compact Convolutional Bayesian Neural Network for Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Deep neural networks have become the standard tool for semantic image segmentation, yet their deterministic formulations give no principled account of what they do not know. Bayesian neural networks address this by treating weights as random variables and propagating uncertainty to the pixel level, but the resulting models are usually obtained by attaching approximate inference to architectures designed for point estimation. Because such backbones carry tens of millions of parameters, and because Bayesian prediction requires several stochastic forward passes per image, the combination is expensive in memory, computation and energy — precisely the resources that are scarce in the robotics, medical and autonomous-driving settings where calibrated uncertainty matters most. We propose ComBiNet, a compact convolutional Bayesian network for image segmentation that is designed from the outset for approximate inference. It couples densely connected feature reuse, dilated convolutions for a wide receptive field without downsampling, and a lightweight encoder–decoder with skip connections, so that accuracy is retained at a fraction of the parameter count. Experiments on CamVid and BDD100K show that ComBiNet matches or exceeds the predictive accuracy of substantially larger Bayesian and non-Bayesian baselines while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters, and that its aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty estimates remain well calibrated and useful for flagging erroneous and out-of-distribution regions. Code is publicly available.

texts.title: Inter Extreme Points Geodesics for Weakly Supervised Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Inter Extreme Points Geodesics for Weakly Supervised Segmentation".
texts.text: We introduce InExtremIS, a weakly supervised 3D approach to train a deep image segmentation network using particularly weak train-time annotations: only 6 extreme clicks at the boundary of the objects of interest. Our fully-automated approach is trained end-to-end and does not require a first stage training on strongly annotated data. Similarly to fully supervised approaches, our method takes advantage of a single-stage training pipeline and requires no segmentation proposal generation. In contrast to existing weakly supervised methods, the extreme points are not only used as hard constraints on the object boundary but also as seeds for generating deep geodesics inside the object. These geodesics, computed on the gradient of a learned feature map rather than on raw intensities, provide dense supervision in the object interior while remaining faithful to image edges. A spatially regularised loss combining a partial cross-entropy term on the geodesics and background constraints with a conditional random field regularisation term propagates this sparse supervision to the whole volume. Experiments were performed on a large open dataset for vestibular schwannoma segmentation from contrast-enhanced T1 and high-resolution T2 MRI. InExtremIS obtained competitive performance, approaching full supervision and outperforming significantly other weakly supervised approaches based on extreme points. Moreover, given a fixed annotation time budget, InExtremIS outperforms full supervision, suggesting that annotating more scans with extreme points is preferable to fully delineating fewer of them. Our code and data are available online.

texts.title: Bayesian dense inverse searching algorithm for real-time stereo matching in minimally invasive surgery
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Bayesian dense inverse searching algorithm for real-time stereo matching in minimally invasive surgery".
texts.text: This paper proposes a CPU-level real-time stereo matching method for surgical images (10 Hz on 640x480 image with a single core of i5-9400). The proposed method is built on the fast "dense inverse searching" algorithm, which estimates the disparity of the stereo images. The overlapping image patches (arbitrary squared image segment) from the images at different scales are aligned based on the photometric consistency presumption. We propose a Bayesian framework to evaluate the probability of the optimized patch disparity at different scales. Moreover, we introduce a spatial Gaussian mixed probability distribution to address the pixel-wise probability within the patch. In the case of a stereo matching, the dense disparity map is estimated by considering both the spatial and temporal constraints, where the temporal consistency is enforced by a Kalman-filter-like propagation of the previous frame's estimate and its uncertainty. This probabilistic treatment allows low-confidence regions -- textureless tissue, specular highlights, smoke and occlusions that are pervasive in minimally invasive surgery -- to be identified and down-weighted rather than producing spurious depth. Extensive experiments on in-vivo and phantom stereo endoscopic datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art learning-based and global optimization approaches while requiring no GPU, no training data and no domain-specific fine-tuning, which is particularly relevant given the scarcity of annotated surgical depth ground truth. The resulting dense, uncertainty-aware depth maps run within the timing budget of intra-operative use and are directly applicable to tissue reconstruction, augmented reality overlay and robotic surgical navigation.

texts.title: RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "RLCorrector: Reinforced Proofreading for Connectomics Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Connectomics aims to reconstruct neural wiring diagrams from high-resolution electron microscopy (EM) volumes, a task that hinges on accurate segmentation of densely packed neurites. Although deep learning has substantially improved automatic segmentation, the results remain imperfect, and the residual split and merge errors must still be repaired by human experts. This proofreading step is now the dominant bottleneck in the connectomics pipeline: it is tedious, expensive, and scales poorly to the terascale volumes produced by modern microscopes. We propose RLCorrector, a reinforcement learning framework that automates proofreading by learning to imitate the decision process of a human proofreader rather than by re-segmenting the data. We cast error correction as a sequential decision problem in which agents inspect a local region of an over- or under-segmented volume and choose merge and split actions that incrementally improve segmentation quality. To handle the two error types and the question of where to look next, we adopt a hierarchical design in which specialized merge and split agents are coordinated by a supervisor agent that allocates attention across candidate error locations, together with reward functions derived from segmentation agreement metrics. Experiments on public EM connectomics datasets show that our method corrects a substantial fraction of residual errors and outperforms baseline correction strategies, reducing the human effort required for reconstruction.

texts.title: High-Resolution Segmentation of Tooth Root Fuzzy Edge Based on Polynomial Curve Fitting with Landmark Detection
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "High-Resolution Segmentation of Tooth Root Fuzzy Edge Based on Polynomial Curve Fitting with Landmark Detection".
texts.text: Accurate delineation of the tooth root is a prerequisite for implant planning, root canal therapy and orthodontic root resorption assessment, yet it remains one of the hardest problems in dental image analysis. Unlike the crown, the root is embedded in alveolar bone of similar radiodensity, and the apical third is thin, tapered and blurred by the partial volume effect, producing a fuzzy edge where pixel-wise classifiers become unstable. Conventional encoder-decoder segmentation networks aggravate this problem: repeated downsampling destroys the very high-frequency detail that defines the apex, and the resulting masks show jagged contours, truncated apices and topologically broken boundaries. We propose a segmentation framework that replaces per-pixel decision making at the fuzzy edge with an explicit geometric boundary model. A high-resolution backbone maintains full-scale feature streams throughout the network, preserving apical detail without the information loss of successive pooling. On top of these features, a landmark detection branch regresses an ordered set of anatomically meaningful control points along the root contour, including the cemento-enamel junction, the mesial and distal root walls and the apical foramen, using heatmap supervision with sub-pixel refinement. The detected landmarks then drive a piecewise polynomial curve fitting module that reconstructs a smooth, continuous and anatomically plausible root boundary, which is fused with the coarse probability map through a curve-guided refinement step. Experiments on cone-beam CT and panoramic radiograph datasets show consistent gains over strong baselines, particularly in boundary-sensitive metrics such as Hausdorff distance and apical localization error, and ablation studies confirm that both the landmark prior and the curve fitting stage contribute independently. The method yields clinically usable root contours in regions where pixel-wise segmentation fails.

texts.title: Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension for Referring Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension for Referring Segmentation".
texts.text: Referring segmentation aims to predict a pixel-level mask for the object or actor described by a natural language expression in an image or a video. Most existing approaches fuse linguistic and visual features in a single step and directly regress the mask, which often fails when several instances of the same category appear and the expression relies on relational cues to disambiguate them. We instead argue that this task should be solved the way humans read such expressions: first perceive every candidate that matches the mentioned category and attributes, and only then exploit relational context to single out the correct one. Following this intuition, we propose a Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension (CMPC) scheme. For images, the CMPC-I module uses entity and attribute words to highlight all plausible candidate entities, then builds a graph over these candidates and propagates information along relational words with graph attention, so that the referent is emphasized while unrelated entities are suppressed. For videos, the CMPC-V module further treats action words as a bridge across frames, connecting candidate tubes over time with temporal graph reasoning to identify the described actor. We additionally introduce a Text-Guided Feature Exchange (TGFE) module that adaptively aggregates multi-level visual features under the guidance of the expression, letting features at different stages refine one another. Extensive experiments on four image and two video referring benchmarks show consistent improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods.

texts.title: Points2Polygons: Context-Based Segmentation from Weak Labels Using Adversarial Networks
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Points2Polygons: Context-Based Segmentation from Weak Labels Using Adversarial Networks".
texts.text: In applied mapping problems, transferring a pretrained segmentation model to a new region or sensor almost always requires new annotations, and dense polygon labels are expensive to produce. Point labels, by contrast, are cheap: an annotator can click object centers an order of magnitude faster than they can trace boundaries. We present Points2Polygons (P2P), a model that learns instance segmentation of small, densely packed objects in overhead imagery from point supervision alone. P2P is built on the observation that the appearance of an object is strongly constrained by its local context, so a network can be taught to hallucinate plausible object extents around labeled points if it is also forced to explain the surrounding background. The model couples a context-based generator with an adversarial discriminator that compares generated segmentations against the local image evidence, together with point-consistency and count constraints that anchor each predicted instance to its annotation. This formulation requires no seed masks, no bounding boxes, and no pretrained segmentation backbone from a related domain. We evaluate P2P on overhead imagery of built structures and agricultural objects across several geographies and ground sample distances, and show that it recovers object footprints with quality approaching fully supervised baselines while using annotations that are substantially cheaper to collect, and that it degrades gracefully as point placement becomes noisy or off-center. We further show that P2P transfers to previously unseen regions given only a small set of points from the target domain, making it practical for rapid adaptation of mapping pipelines to new areas of interest.

texts.title: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Food Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "A Large-Scale Benchmark for Food Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Food image understanding has become a core problem in multimedia and health computing, underpinning applications from automated dietary assessment to recipe retrieval and restaurant recommendation. Most existing work, however, treats food recognition as an image-level classification task, which cannot answer the finer-grained questions that matter in practice: which ingredients are present in a dish, and how much of each. Progress on pixel-level food understanding has been held back by the lack of suitable data: publicly available segmentation datasets for food are small, annotate only whole dishes rather than their constituents, or cover a narrow set of cuisines. In this paper we introduce a large-scale benchmark for food image segmentation, consisting of thousands of everyday food photographs annotated with pixel-wise ingredient masks spanning over one hundred ingredient categories and hundreds of distinct dishes, with several ingredients labeled per image on average. We describe the collection and annotation protocol, including the category taxonomy and the quality-control steps used to cope with the deformable, occluded and visually ambiguous appearance that makes ingredients unusually hard to delineate. We benchmark representative semantic segmentation architectures on the dataset and further show that injecting recipe-level textual knowledge into the visual encoder improves ingredient-level accuracy over purely visual baselines. Our analysis indicates that food segmentation remains far from solved and exposes failure modes, such as fine-grained confusion among visually similar ingredients, that are underrepresented in generic segmentation benchmarks. The dataset and code are publicly released to support future research.

texts.title: Deep Active Contours Using Locally Controlled Distance Vector Flow
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Deep Active Contours Using Locally Controlled Distance Vector Flow".
texts.text: Active contour models (ACMs) have long been used for image segmentation, but their practical use is limited by the need for manual initialization, a narrow capture range, and hand-tuned energy weights that must be re-adjusted for every image domain. Recent work couples convolutional neural networks with ACMs so that the network, rather than a human operator, supplies the parameters of the energy functional; nevertheless, initialization is typically still manual, and results remain highly sensitive to where the initial contour is placed, often leading to poor convergence at weak or concave boundaries. We present a fully automatic deep active contour framework that addresses initialization, capture range, and boundary convergence jointly. Two convolutional networks are trained in tandem: the first predicts a coarse segmentation mask, from which we derive a distance transform and an automatically placed initial contour, while the second predicts spatially varying (locally controlled) weights for the length, region, and external energy terms at every contour node. From the predicted distance transform we construct a locally controlled distance vector flow field in which each pixel carries a vector pointing toward the nearest predicted boundary point with magnitude given by the Euclidean distance map. Unlike conventional gradient vector flow, this field is dense, non-vanishing far from edges, and free of the diffusion-induced smoothing that erodes concavities, so it extends the capture range across the whole image while preserving the geometric detail needed for accurate delineation. The contour is evolved differentiably, allowing the two networks to be optimized end to end with a segmentation loss defined directly on the final polygon. We evaluate the method on two building-footprint instance segmentation benchmarks (Vaihingen and Bing Huts) and two mammography datasets (INbreast and DDSM-BCRP). The proposed approach improves mean intersection-over-union and, in particular, boundary F-score over recent deep active contour baselines, and achieves Dice similarity coefficients competitive with state-of-the-art segmentation frameworks on the mammography data, while requiring no user interaction and no dataset-specific parameter tuning. Ablation studies confirm that both automatic initialization from the predicted distance transform and the locally controlled vector flow contribute independently to the observed gains, with the largest improvements appearing on objects with concave or elongated structure where classical vector flow fields fail to propagate.

texts.title: A Generalized Asymmetric Dual-front Model for Active Contours and Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "A Generalized Asymmetric Dual-front Model for Active Contours and Image Segmentation".
texts.text: The Voronoi diagram-based dual-front scheme is a powerful and efficient way to carry out curve evolution for image segmentation, in which the evolving contours are taken to be the interfaces between adjacent Voronoi regions induced by geodesic distance maps. Its behaviour is therefore governed entirely by the geodesic metric used to measure curve length, which in existing formulations is built from isotropic or symmetric anisotropic image features and consequently exploits only a limited portion of the available image information. In this paper, we introduce a generalized asymmetric dual-front model whose front propagation is driven by a family of asymmetric quadratic metrics. These metrics blend several complementary cues in a single geodesic framework: edge-based anisotropy and directionality, an asymmetry term derived from the image gradient that encourages contours to align with object boundaries in a prescribed orientation, region-based homogeneity terms that exploit appearance statistics of the regions separated by the evolving curve, and a curvature-penalized component that favours smooth and regular segmentation boundaries. The resulting geodesic distance maps are computed efficiently by a variant of the fast marching method adapted to asymmetric quadratic metrics, so that each dual-front update remains inexpensive. Experiments on synthetic and natural images, including comparisons with state-of-the-art active contour approaches, show that the proposed model is accurate, robust to contour initialization and to the placement of the narrowband region, and able to handle objects with weak, blurred or partially missing boundaries as well as strong background clutter.

texts.title: A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy".
texts.text: Performing exact inference in graphs is a recurring task in machine learning, arising in problems such as image segmentation, community detection, and correlation clustering. Given an undirected connected graph and a single noisy observation of each edge, the goal is to exactly recover an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes. This problem can be cast as a quadratic combinatorial optimization over the Boolean hypercube, which is NP-hard in general, and is therefore commonly attacked by convex relaxations. The degree-2 relaxation from the sum-of-squares hierarchy, i.e., the standard semidefinite program, has been studied extensively and its exact recovery behavior is well characterized in terms of a spectral quantity of the graph. The degree-4 relaxation is provably tighter and succeeds in regimes where the degree-2 relaxation fails, but it is generally dismissed as computationally prohibitive, since it optimizes over a matrix whose dimension grows quadratically with the number of nodes. In this work we give a thorough view of the degree-4 case. We exploit the structure of the moment matrix to obtain a low-rank, Burer-Monteiro-style parameterization, and we analyze a projected gradient method over this non-convex landscape, establishing a per-iteration cost and a linear convergence rate to a solution from which the ground truth is read off. On the statistical side, we derive sufficient conditions for exact recovery that depend on the connectivity of the graph and on the noise level, and we show analytically that these conditions are weaker than the best known conditions for the degree-2 relaxation, quantifying the gain of moving one level up the hierarchy. We also clarify when the extra level does not help, characterizing graph families for which the two relaxations share the same recovery threshold. Experiments on synthetic graphs corroborate our theory and illustrate the predicted separation between the two levels of the hierarchy.

texts.title: Rethinking BiSeNet For Real-time Semantic Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Rethinking BiSeNet For Real-time Semantic Segmentation".
texts.text: BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve 71.9% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti, which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0 FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

texts.title: Bayesian Logistic Shape Model Inference: application to cochlea image segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Bayesian Logistic Shape Model Inference: application to cochlea image segmentation".
texts.text: Segmenting small and thin anatomical structures from clinical images is an ill-posed problem: the voxel size is of the same order as the structure itself, contrast is weak, and partial volume effects blur the boundaries. Statistical shape models are an effective way of regularizing such problems, but conventional model fitting returns a single point estimate and no measure of confidence, which is problematic when the resulting shape is used to derive clinical measurements. We introduce a Bayesian formulation of shape model inference based on a logistic shape representation. A shape is encoded implicitly by a signed distance-like function constrained to a low-dimensional linear subspace learned from a set of segmented surfaces, and a logistic transform maps that function to voxelwise membership probabilities. Image observations are then modeled as Bernoulli variables, which yields a likelihood that is smooth and differentiable with respect to both shape and pose parameters and that accounts explicitly for partial volume voxels rather than treating them as noise. Together with Gaussian priors on the shape coefficients and on the similarity transform, this defines a posterior distribution over shapes that we characterize with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, using a Laplace approximation at the maximum a posteriori estimate to precondition the sampler. The framework also allows the intensity-to-probability mapping and the model hyperparameters to be estimated jointly with the shape. We apply the approach to cochlea segmentation from clinical computed tomography, where the scala tympani and scala vestibuli are not resolvable at the acquired resolution. The method achieves segmentation accuracy comparable to or better than deterministic shape model fitting and deep learning baselines, while additionally providing credible intervals on derived quantities such as cochlear duct length, a measurement used for electrode array selection in cochlear implant surgery. The posterior spread is shown to be informative, growing where the image evidence is weakest and correlating with the actual error of the estimate.

texts.title: GENESIS-V2: Inferring Unordered Object Representations without Iterative Refinement
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "GENESIS-V2: Inferring Unordered Object Representations without Iterative Refinement".
texts.text: Advances in unsupervised learning of object-centric representations promise to endow machines with a compositional understanding of visual scenes, but the leading approaches rely on machinery that limits their applicability. Methods such as iterative variational inference and Slot Attention infer a set of latent slots by running a fixed number of refinement steps over a fixed number of slots, which fixes object capacity ahead of time, adds computational overhead, and can be difficult to optimise; models that instead impose an ordering on slots, as in sequential attention or autoregressive priors, break the permutation symmetry of the underlying scene description. We introduce GENESIS-V2, a generative model of scenes that infers a variable number of unordered object representations in a single forward pass, without iterative refinement. Its core is a novel, fully differentiable attention mechanism inspired by non-probabilistic instance segmentation: pixel embeddings are randomly seeded and clustered through an instance colouring stick-breaking process, yielding attention masks whose number is not fixed a priori and whose ordering carries no information. We evaluate GENESIS-V2 on synthetic benchmarks and on two challenging real-world datasets of robotic manipulation scenes, where it outperforms prior object-centric generative models in segmentation quality and generative performance while remaining competitive at unsupervised scene decomposition and image synthesis.

texts.title: Semantic Segmentation with Generative Models: Semi-Supervised Learning and Strong Out-of-Domain Generalization
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semantic Segmentation with Generative Models: Semi-Supervised Learning and Strong Out-of-Domain Generalization".
texts.text: Training deep networks for semantic segmentation requires large amounts of densely annotated data, and pixel-level labels are among the most expensive annotations to collect. We show that generative adversarial networks trained for image synthesis already encode, in their intermediate feature maps, a representation that is remarkably well suited for dense prediction: because the generator must produce every pixel of a coherent scene, its latent features carry semantic, part-level, and depth-ordering information that can be decoded into segmentation masks with very little supervision. Building on this observation, we propose a simple approach that turns a pretrained GAN into a semantic segmentation branch by attaching a lightweight decoder to the generator's features and training it on a handful of labeled examples. Because the resulting segmenter lives inside the generator, it produces an infinite stream of image-annotation pairs: sampling a latent code yields both a synthetic image and its predicted label map. We use this synthetic dataset to train an off-the-shelf segmentation network that operates directly on real images at test time, which both closes the gap to the generative model and makes inference independent of it. On several benchmarks our method matches or outperforms strong semi-supervised baselines while using as few as 16 annotated images, and in some settings approaches fully supervised performance trained with two orders of magnitude more labels. Most strikingly, the resulting segmenters generalize far outside the training distribution: models trained only on synthetic photographs transfer to paintings, sketches, cartoons, statues, and heavily corrupted inputs with substantially smaller degradation than their fully supervised counterparts, which we attribute to the diversity and smooth coverage of the generator's latent space. We analyze which layers of the generator carry the most label-relevant information, study how performance scales with the number of annotated latents, and show that the same recipe applies across object categories and generator architectures. We further introduce an out-of-domain benchmark to quantify robustness under distribution shift and release it alongside our code, and we discuss failure modes arising from biases inherited from the generator's training data.

texts.title: Ensemble Learning based on Classifier Prediction Confidence and Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimisation for polyp localisation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Ensemble Learning based on Classifier Prediction Confidence and Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimisation for polyp localisation".
texts.text: Colorectal cancer is one of the deadliest malignancies worldwide, and early detection and removal of adenomatous polyps during colonoscopy substantially reduces mortality. Automated polyp localisation is therefore an important component of computer-aided diagnosis, yet single detectors remain unreliable: polyps vary widely in size, shape, texture and colour, they are often partially occluded or blurred, and each network architecture tends to fail on a different subset of frames. Ensemble learning can compensate for these individual weaknesses, but naive fusion of detections treats all base learners as equally competent and can degrade performance when weak members dominate. This paper proposes an ensemble framework for polyp localisation that combines the outputs of several heterogeneous object detectors using their prediction confidence as the basis for fusion. Candidate bounding boxes from the base learners are clustered and merged, and each learner contributes according to a weight reflecting how trustworthy its confidence scores are. Because these weights, together with the confidence and overlap thresholds that govern fusion, define a large non-convex search space, they are optimised with Comprehensive Learning Particle Swarm Optimisation (CLPSO), whose comprehensive learning strategy preserves swarm diversity and avoids the premature convergence typical of standard PSO on high-dimensional, multimodal problems. The method is evaluated on public colonoscopy benchmarks under both still-image and video protocols, and compared against the individual base detectors, conventional fusion rules and alternative weight-search strategies. Results show consistent improvements in precision, recall and F1-score, indicating that confidence-aware, CLPSO-tuned fusion is an effective and architecture-agnostic way to improve polyp localisation.

texts.title: FANet: A Feedback Attention Network for Improved Biomedical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "FANet: A Feedback Attention Network for Improved Biomedical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: The increase of available large clinical and experimental datasets has contributed to a substantial amount of important contributions in the area of biomedical image analysis. Image segmentation, which is crucial for any quantitative analysis, has especially attracted attention. Recent hardware advancement has led to the success of deep learning approaches. However, although deep learning models are being trained on large datasets, existing methods do not use the information from different learning epochs effectively. In this work, we leverage the information already learned by the model during training to further improve its prediction quality. We propose a feedback attention network (FANet) that unifies the previous epoch mask with the feature map of the current training epoch. The previous epoch mask is then used to provide hard attention to the learned feature maps at different convolutional layers. The network also allows rectifying the predictions iteratively during the test time. We show that our proposed feedback attention model provides a substantial improvement on most segmentation metrics tested on seven publicly available biomedical imaging datasets demonstrating the effectiveness of FANet. The proposed method achieves a dice coefficient of 0.8752, 0.9210, 0.9114, 0.9089, 0.9166, 0.9210, and 0.8321 on the Kvasir-SEG, CVC-ClinicDB, 2018 Data Science Bowl, ISIC 2018, EM, DRIVE, and CVC-ColonDB datasets, respectively, outperforming competitive baselines such as U-Net, U-Net++, ResUNet++, and attention-based architectures. Extensive ablation studies confirm that the gains stem from the feedback mechanism rather than added capacity, and that iterative test-time refinement yields consistent improvements in boundary delineation for small and low-contrast structures.

texts.title: Self-Guided and Cross-Guided Learning for Few-Shot Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Self-Guided and Cross-Guided Learning for Few-Shot Segmentation".
texts.text: Few-shot segmentation aims to segment novel object categories in a query image given only a handful of annotated support images. Most existing methods condense each support image into a single prototype through masked global average pooling, and then match it against the query features. We observe that this compression is lossy: the resulting prototype is dominated by the most discriminative parts of the object, so the information carried by the remaining regions is largely discarded, which in turn leads to incomplete query predictions. To address this, we propose a self-guided learning approach. By making an initial prediction on the annotated support image itself, the support mask is decomposed into the region that the primary prototype already covers and the region it misses, from which a primary prototype and an auxiliary prototype are generated respectively. By aggregating both prototypes, the support information is described far more completely, which yields better segmentation of the query image. Furthermore, we propose a cross-guided module for multi-shot segmentation, in which the prediction quality of each support image is used to weight and fuse the final query predictions, so that high-quality supports dominate and low-quality ones are suppressed without retraining the model. Experiments on PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art performance.

texts.title: Pneumothorax Segmentation: Deep Learning Image Segmentation to predict Pneumothorax
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Pneumothorax Segmentation: Deep Learning Image Segmentation to predict Pneumothorax".
texts.text: Pneumothorax, the abnormal collection of air in the pleural space, can progress within minutes from an incidental finding to a life-threatening tension pneumothorax. Diagnosis is made primarily from chest radiographs, but the visual cue is often a faint, low-contrast pleural line that is easily missed under time pressure, and confirmation depends on the availability of an experienced radiologist. This paper investigates whether deep learning image segmentation can both detect pneumothorax and delineate its extent, producing a pixel-level mask that is verifiable by a clinician rather than an opaque image-level label. We frame the problem as binary semantic segmentation and train an encoder-decoder network of the U-Net family, using an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional backbone as the encoder to compensate for limited annotated medical data. Experiments are performed on the SIIM-ACR Pneumothorax dataset of chest radiographs with run-length-encoded expert annotations, in which the large majority of images are negative and positive masks occupy only a small fraction of the image area. We address this severe foreground-background imbalance with a composite binary cross-entropy and soft Dice objective, stratified sampling, intensity and geometric augmentation, and a post-processing stage that tunes the binarization threshold and suppresses small spurious components. Performance is reported using the Dice similarity coefficient, together with image-level sensitivity and specificity, and is compared against classification-only and plain U-Net baselines. The segmentation model improves mask overlap and reduces false positives on negative studies, and an ablation study isolates the contribution of pretraining, loss design, input resolution, and post-processing. The results suggest that segmentation-based models are a practical basis for radiograph triage, flagging suspected pneumothorax and showing the evidence for the prediction, while the remaining errors concentrate on small apical collections and cases with chest tubes or subcutaneous emphysema, which we identify as the priority for future work.

texts.title: Deep Neural Networks Learn Meta-Structures to Segment Fluorescence Microscopy Images
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Deep Neural Networks Learn Meta-Structures to Segment Fluorescence Microscopy Images".
texts.text: Fluorescence microscopy images are routinely segmented with deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on large sets of pixel-accurate annotations, yet it remains unclear what information in those annotations the networks actually exploit. Here we probe this question by systematically degrading the training masks of standard segmentation architectures. We find that networks trained on masks whose object boundaries have been heavily perturbed, dilated, eroded, or replaced by coarse geometric proxies still segment test images with accuracy close to that of networks trained on ground-truth masks, and that the resulting predictions recover sharp boundaries the training data never contained. Performance collapses only when the annotations no longer preserve the approximate location, extent, and spatial arrangement of the objects. We term this preserved, boundary-independent information the meta-structure of the sample, and formalize it as a low-dimensional description of where objects are and how they are distributed relative to one another and to the image background.
