Guided by this notion, we construct meta-structure annotations that are far cheaper to produce than delineated masks and show that they support segmentation performance comparable to conventional training on several fluorescence microscopy datasets spanning different subcellular and tissue-level targets. These results indicate that DNN segmentation of fluorescence images is driven largely by learned meta-structural priors rather than by precise boundary supervision, and suggest a practical route to reducing the annotation burden in biomedical image analysis.

texts.title: K-Net: Towards Unified Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "K-Net: Towards Unified Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation have largely been advanced by task-specific frameworks, despite the fact that all three reduce to the same underlying operation: partitioning an image into a set of meaningful pixel groups. We present K-Net, a single framework that unifies the three tasks through a set of learnable kernels, where each kernel is responsible for generating the mask of either one potential instance or one stuff class. Static kernels alone are too weak to cope with the highly varied appearance of objects across images, so we introduce a kernel update strategy that makes every kernel dynamic and conditional on the pixel group it currently activates, progressively refining kernels and their masks together. The assignment between kernels and targets is learned end-to-end with bipartite matching, which makes K-Net naturally box-free and NMS-free. K-Net achieves 55.2% PQ on the MS COCO panoptic segmentation test-dev split and 54.3% mIoU on the ADE20K semantic segmentation validation set, surpassing previously published single-model results on both, while matching the instance segmentation accuracy of Cascade Mask R-CNN on MS COCO with 60%-90% faster inference speeds.

texts.title: Towards Learning Food Portion From Monocular Images With Cross-Domain Feature Adaptation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Towards Learning Food Portion From Monocular Images With Cross-Domain Feature Adaptation".
texts.text: Estimating food portion size from a single monocular image is a critical step toward image-based dietary assessment, yet it remains challenging because a 2D projection discards the scale and depth cues needed to recover volume, and because paired image-to-energy training data are scarce and expensive to collect. In this work we address the problem of directly predicting the energy content of an eating occasion from one RGB image without relying on fiducial markers, depth sensors, or user-provided reference objects. We propose a deep regression framework that fuses two complementary representations: appearance features extracted from the RGB image, and features extracted from a learned "energy distribution map," an intermediate spatial representation that assigns energy density to image regions and thereby makes the mapping from pixels to calories more explicit. Because real eating occasion images with ground truth energy labels are limited, we additionally leverage a large set of synthetically generated images with exact energy annotations, and we introduce a cross-domain feature adaptation strategy with feature normalization that aligns the representations learned from the synthetic and real domains so that knowledge transfers without the network overfitting to rendering artifacts. Experiments on an eating occasion image dataset collected in a community dwelling feeding study show that the proposed method improves over single-domain and RGB-only baselines, achieving a mean absolute error of 40.05 kCal and a mean absolute percentage error of 11.47% for energy estimation. These results suggest that combining learned energy distribution cues with cross-domain adaptation is a promising direction for practical, sensor-free dietary assessment from everyday photographs.

texts.title: Learning to Segment from Scribbles using Multi-scale Adversarial Attention Gates
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Learning to Segment from Scribbles using Multi-scale Adversarial Attention Gates".
texts.text: Large, fully-annotated datasets are the main driver of progress in medical image segmentation, but obtaining dense pixel-level labels is expensive, slow, and requires expert knowledge. Learning from scribbles — sparse, quickly drawn strokes marking a few pixels of each class — is an attractive alternative, yet scribbles carry no information about object extent or shape, so models trained on them tend to leak across boundaries and produce anatomically implausible masks. We address this by regularising a scribble-supervised segmentor with an adversarial shape prior, learned from a set of unpaired segmentation masks that need not correspond to the training images and can be reused across datasets. Rather than applying the adversarial signal only at the output, we propose multi-scale adversarial attention gates: the discriminator's assessment of shape realism is fed back into the segmentor as attention maps that modulate its features at several resolutions, progressively suppressing activations that would yield unrealistic structures while letting the sparse scribble supervision refine local detail. The resulting model is a single-stage, end-to-end trainable network with negligible inference overhead. On cardiac MRI (ACDC, LVSC), abdominal CT/MRI (CHAOS), and pedestrian parsing (PPSS) benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms strong weakly-supervised baselines and approaches fully-supervised performance while using only a small fraction of the annotation effort. We also release scribble annotations for the cardiac datasets and make our code publicly available.

texts.title: FedDG: Federated Domain Generalization on Medical Image Segmentation via Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "FedDG: Federated Domain Generalization on Medical Image Segmentation via Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space".
texts.text: Federated learning allows multiple medical institutions to jointly train a segmentation model without sharing patient data, but the resulting model is usually evaluated on the same institutions that contributed to training. In practice, a deployed model must also work at hospitals that never took part in federated training, where scanners, protocols and populations differ. We study this problem, which we term federated domain generalization: learning from multiple decentralized source domains so that the model generalizes to a completely unseen target domain. The setting is harder than conventional domain generalization because each client is confined to its own local data and cannot access images from other clients, so the cross-domain variation that generalization methods normally exploit is inaccessible. We address this with a continuous frequency space interpolation mechanism that exchanges only the amplitude spectrum of images across clients, leaving the phase spectrum, which carries the semantic content, on the local site; each client can therefore synthesize images spanning a continuum of distributions while respecting privacy constraints. On top of this augmented space we design an episodic learning scheme with boundary-oriented and background-relevant meta-objectives that explicitly regularizes segmentation structure under distribution shift. Experiments on retinal fundus optic disc/cup segmentation and prostate MRI segmentation show consistent gains over federated and generalization baselines.

texts.title: Contrastive Registration for Unsupervised Medical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Contrastive Registration for Unsupervised Medical Image Segmentation".
texts.text:
Deep learning has become the dominant paradigm for medical image segmentation, yet its success rests on large collections of voxel-wise annotations that are expensive to obtain, require clinical expertise, and generalise poorly across scanners, protocols and anatomies. Registration-based label propagation offers an appealing alternative, since a single annotated atlas can in principle segment an entire cohort by deforming its labels onto unlabelled scans. In practice, however, such approaches are limited by the objective that drives the registration: intensity-based similarity metrics are unreliable under low tissue contrast, intensity inhomogeneity and inter-subject variability, so the resulting deformation fields align appearance rather than anatomy, and propagated labels drift at structure boundaries.

In this work we introduce a contrastive registration framework for unsupervised medical image segmentation, which learns deformation and segmentation jointly without any ground-truth masks for the target images. Our key idea is to drive registration in a learned representation space rather than in intensity space: a contrastive objective pulls together the features of anatomically corresponding locations in the moving and fixed images while pushing apart features of distinct structures, yielding embeddings that are discriminative of anatomy and invariant to appearance. We couple this objective with a deformation model that aggregates non-local context, so that global anatomical layout constrains local correspondence, and with a consistency term that ties the propagated labels to the predicted segmentation.

We evaluate the framework on multi-centre cardiac MRI and abdominal CT benchmarks. The proposed method consistently improves over unsupervised registration, clustering and self-supervised segmentation baselines, approaches the performance of supervised models trained with limited annotation, and transfers across imaging centres without retraining. Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the contrastive objective, the non-local deformation model and the consistency term, and analyse robustness to atlas choice and to the number of negatives.

texts.title: Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation through Dual-task Consistency
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation through Dual-task Consistency".
texts.text: Deep learning has achieved strong results in medical image segmentation, but training such models usually demands large collections of pixel-level annotations, which are costly and time-consuming for clinical experts to produce. Semi-supervised learning mitigates this burden by exploiting abundant unlabeled scans, and most existing approaches do so by encouraging predictions to remain stable under data-level or model-level perturbations. In this work, we argue that consistency can also be imposed at the task level. We present a dual-task consistency framework in which a single network jointly predicts a pixel-wise segmentation probability map and a geometry-aware level set representation of the target. A differentiable task transform layer converts the predicted level set function into an approximate segmentation map, so that a consistency loss between the two task outputs can be computed on any image, labeled or not. Unlabeled scans therefore regularize the model directly, pushing it toward predictions that are simultaneously accurate and geometrically plausible, while the supervised loss is applied only to the annotated subset. Experiments on two public 3D benchmarks, left atrium MRI and pancreas CT, show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches, with especially large gains when only a small fraction of the scans are annotated. The framework is simple, efficient, and readily extended to other pairs of related tasks. Code is publicly available.

texts.title: Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Supervision: A Review of Deep Network Models
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Medical Image Segmentation with Limited Supervision: A Review of Deep Network Models".
texts.text: Despite the success of deep learning in medical image segmentation, the prevailing fully supervised paradigm depends on large collections of pixel- or voxel-level annotations that are costly to obtain, require scarce clinical expertise, and are frequently affected by inter-observer variability. This has motivated a rapidly expanding body of work on segmentation models that learn from limited supervision. In this review, we survey deep network models designed to operate under annotation scarcity and organize them within a unified taxonomy spanning semi-supervised learning, weakly supervised learning with image-level labels, points, scribbles and bounding boxes, self-supervised and unsupervised pre-training, transfer learning and domain adaptation, few-shot and one-shot segmentation, and learning with noisy or sparse labels. For each family, we describe the underlying assumptions and the mechanisms by which unlabeled or coarsely labeled data are exploited, including consistency regularization and perturbation-based training, pseudo-labeling and self-training, co-training and mutual learning, adversarial and generative modeling, contrastive and masked-image pre-training, class activation maps and seed-expansion strategies, anatomical priors and shape constraints, uncertainty estimation, and label-efficient data augmentation and synthesis. We further review architectural backbones ranging from encoder-decoder convolutional networks to transformer-based and hybrid designs, and discuss how recent vision foundation models and promptable segmentation are reshaping the annotation-efficiency landscape. Commonly used benchmarks across modalities such as MRI, CT, ultrasound, X-ray, histopathology and endoscopy are summarized together with evaluation protocols, and we highlight recurring methodological issues that hinder fair comparison, including inconsistent labeled-data splits, backbone mismatches, and under-reported baselines. We conclude by identifying open challenges, including robustness to domain shift, calibration and trustworthiness, class imbalance and small-lesion segmentation, volumetric and multi-modal settings, computational cost, and clinical validation, and outline directions for developing annotation-efficient segmentation methods suitable for deployment in practice.

texts.title: EMDS-5: Environmental Microorganism Image Dataset Fifth Version for Multiple Image Analysis Tasks
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "EMDS-5: Environmental Microorganism Image Dataset Fifth Version for Multiple Image Analysis Tasks".
texts.text: Environmental microorganisms (EMs) are widely used as indicators of water and soil quality, but their identification still relies heavily on manual microscopic examination, which is slow, costly and dependent on expert experience. Computer-aided analysis offers an alternative, yet progress has been limited by the scarcity of public microscopic image datasets that support more than a single analysis task. To address this gap, we present EMDS-5, the fifth version of the Environmental Microorganism Image Dataset. EMDS-5 contains 21 EM categories, each with 20 original microscopic images together with their corresponding manually labelled ground truth images, giving 420 original images and their paired annotations. Compared with earlier versions, EMDS-5 enlarges the number of categories and images, improves the quality and consistency of the ground truth annotations, and provides both single-object and multi-object labelling, so that the same data can serve image preprocessing, denoising, edge detection, image segmentation, feature extraction, object detection, image classification and content-based image retrieval. To demonstrate the usability of the dataset, we carry out a series of baseline experiments covering classical and deep learning methods for these tasks and report their evaluation results. EMDS-5 is freely available to the research community and is intended to support the development and fair comparison of EM image analysis methods.

texts.title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Network with Category-Centric Prototype Aligner for Biomedical Image Segmentation
texts.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Network with Category-Centric Prototype Aligner for Biomedical Image Segmentation".
texts.text: Deep convolutional networks deliver strong biomedical image segmentation accuracy, but a model trained on one imaging modality usually degrades sharply on another because of the severe appearance shift between acquisition protocols, and dense expert annotation of every new modality is prohibitively costly. Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses this by transferring knowledge from a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain, yet most adversarial approaches align only the marginal feature distributions of the two domains. Such domain-level alignment is agnostic to semantics: features belonging to different anatomical categories may be mapped onto one another, yielding representations that are statistically well matched but semantically entangled, which is especially damaging for small, thin, or low-contrast structures. We propose an unsupervised domain adaptation network equipped with a category-centric prototype aligner that makes adaptation explicitly class-conditional. Image-level appearance translation first narrows the low-level gap, after which a shared encoder embeds both domains into a common space where a class prototype is maintained as the centroid of its features and updated by an exponential moving average across mini-batches, using ground-truth masks for the source and confidence-filtered pseudo labels for the target. A bidirectional alignment objective draws target features toward the corresponding source prototype while repelling prototypes of distinct categories, and an uncertainty-guided weighting scheme down-weights unreliable target predictions to limit error accumulation. Experiments on cross-modality cardiac substructure and abdominal multi-organ segmentation show consistent gains in Dice and surface distance over state-of-the-art adaptation methods, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component.
